opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a fairly honest observation about how these models actually work. Generative AI today is extraordinarily good at things that look like what it has seen before. When a problem sits within the distribution of its training data, even loosely, the model can interpolate remarkably well, sometimes in ways that feel almost magical. But when you push it slightly outside that distribution, with an unusual reasoning problem, a strange combination of constraints, or a commonsense situation that's rarely written down, it can fail in surprisingly brittle and even silly ways.

So there are two broad ways to respond to that. One is to hope that scaling alone will eventually produce true generalization, that the model will learn to extrapolate the way humans do. I'm not saying that's impossible, but I'm skeptical it happens automatically. The other, more pragmatic approach is to recognize that if the model mostly does well in-distribution, then a powerful lever is to expand what counts as in-distribution. You systematically find where the model breaks, the long tail of cases, and you create data, often synthetic, carefully generated and filtered, that covers those gaps. What used to be out-of-distribution becomes familiar territory.

That's partly why I've been so interested in synthetic data and in methods like symbolic knowledge distillation, where you don't just scrape more of the internet but deliberately craft the data you need. The internet is huge but very skewed. It overrepresents some things and almost never spells out the obvious commonsense knowledge humans take for granted, precisely because it's obvious to us. So the model never sees it stated explicitly.

There's also a deeper point. I don't think this is merely a hack. Humans, too, become competent by turning the unfamiliar into the familiar through practice, exposure, and reflection. The difference is that we're far more data-efficient. So while I'd love to see more fundamental progress on generalization itself, in the meantime, being thoughtful and intentional about the data, and about filling in the parts of the distribution that matter, is one of the most effective ways to make these models more robust, more reliable, and frankly, smaller and more efficient too. You don't necessarily need a giant model if you've given a smaller one the right data.

r002.rationale: It says humans can make the unfamiliar familiar through practice and exposure, but does not state that humans handle driving corner cases without seeing many examples.

r003.rationale: The response discusses synthetic data and expanding training coverage, but does not mention reinforcement learning or model exploration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so here's the thing. If you look at where today's models shine and where they fall flat, the pattern is really consistent. They're remarkable on the kinds of problems that look like what they've seen during pretraining, and they get surprisingly brittle the moment you step a little bit outside that. And I don't think that's a bug that goes away with more scale. I think it's intrinsic to what these models are. They're fundamentally distribution learners. They interpolate beautifully within the space of the data, and they extrapolate poorly beyond it.

So the question for me became, okay, if that's the nature of the beast, what's the lever we actually have? And one answer, which sounds almost too simple, is: stop asking the model to extrapolate. Take the cases that are currently out of distribution and make them in distribution. In other words, the frontier isn't only about bigger models. It's about shaping the data so that the hard, weird, long-tail stuff the model keeps tripping over becomes ordinary to it.

Now, that's easier said than done, because the whole reason those cases are out of distribution is that they're rare in the web. Nobody writes down the obvious commonsense inferences, nobody writes down the failure modes of their own reasoning. So you can't just scrape more of it. You have to synthesize it, or elicit it, in a targeted way. And that's where a lot of my work has gone. You can use models themselves as a kind of generator, you can use critics and verifiers to filter, you can distill from a large model into a small one in a way that's actually quite surgical about what gap you're trying to close. It's a little bit like, instead of sending a student to read the entire library and hoping they absorb what they need, you figure out what they don't know and you write the textbook chapter on exactly that.

And what I find exciting about this framing is that it changes the research question. The question is no longer just "can we make the model bigger" but "can we characterize the distribution of what the model gets wrong, and can we close that gap deliberately." That's a question where smaller labs, academics, people without a hundred thousand GPUs can actually contribute, because the leverage is in the cleverness of the data, not the brute force of the compute. And frankly, I think it's also where some of the more interesting questions about what these models really understand live, because when you try to make something in-distribution, you're forced to confront what the model is actually missing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says models excel on problems that look like what they saw during pretraining.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss humans handling driving corner cases without many examples.

r003.rationale: It discusses targeted synthesis, critics, and distillation, but not reinforcement learning or the model exploring to bring cases into distribution.

astra-6.text:
Because these models are very good at learning patterns from the data they’ve seen, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they can handle a situation that’s meaningfully different. And in the real world, those situations come up all the time. We can change just a small detail in a question, and suddenly something that looked like robust reasoning falls apart.

So making out-of-distribution cases in-distribution is a way of expanding the range of situations the model can learn from. That doesn’t have to mean collecting more of the same internet text. It can mean creating examples that expose a missing concept, challenge a shortcut, or require the model to apply knowledge in a different context.

But there’s a catch: we can’t anticipate every possible situation. So the goal isn’t simply to memorize more cases. It’s to use that broader experience to learn principles that transfer. Otherwise, we’re just moving the boundary of where the model fails, without really improving its ability to reason beyond what it has seen.

r001.rationale: It says models are very good at learning patterns from data they have seen and can fail when a situation differs, conveying stronger performance on familiar cases.

r002.rationale: It does not mention humans, driving, or handling corner cases without many examples.

r003.rationale: It discusses expanding training examples and learning transferable principles, but does not mention reinforcement learning or model-driven exploration.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the real world is full of situations that are a little different from what you have seen before. You cannot enumerate all the possible situations and put them into the training data. So if our approach is always to collect more examples whenever a model fails, we're going to be chasing this forever.

What we really want is for a model to learn underlying principles that let it connect a new situation to things it already understands. Something can be out of distribution at the level of the exact words or scenario, but familiar at the level of the concepts involved. Humans do this all the time: we encounter something new, but we can reason about it using what we already know.

So making out-of-distribution cases in-distribution is not just about expanding the dataset. It's about learning representations and reasoning abilities that make unfamiliar situations understandable. That's central to getting beyond models that are very fluent in familiar settings but surprisingly brittle when something changes.
